Abstract:
Dexterous manipulation, which refers to the ability of a robotic hand or multi-fingered end-effector to skillfully control, reorient, and manipulate objects through precise, coordinated finger movements and adaptive force modulation, enables complex interactions similar to human hand dexterity. With recent advances in robotics and machine learning, there is a growing demand for these systems to operate in complex and unstructured environments. Traditional model-based approaches struggle to generalize across tasks and object variations due to the high dimensionality and complex contact dynamics of dexterous manipulation. Although model-free methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) show promise, they require extensive training, large-scale interaction data, and carefully designed rewards for stability and effectiveness. Imitation learning (IL) offers an alternative by allowing robots to acquire dexterous manipulation skills directly from expert demonstrations, capturing fine-grained coordination and contact dynamics while bypassing the need for explicit modeling and large-scale trial-and-error. This survey provides an overview of dexterous manipulation methods based on imitation learning, details recent advances, and addresses key challenges in the field. Additionally, it explores potential research directions to enhance IL-driven dexterous manipulation. Our goal is to offer researchers and practitioners a comprehensive introduction to this rapidly evolving domain.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Dexterous manipulation is a crucial yet highly complex challenge in humanoid robotics, demanding precise, adaptable, and sample-efficient learning methods. As humanoid robots are usually designed to operate in human-centric environments and interact with everyday objects, mastering dexterous manipulation is critical for real-world deployment. Traditional approaches, such as reinforcement learning and imitation learning, have made significant strides, but they often struggle due to the unique challenges of real-world dexterous manipulation, including high-dimensional control, limited training data, and covariate shift. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of these challenges and reviews existing learning-based methods for real-world dexterous manipulation, spanning imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid approaches. A promising yet underexplored direction is interactive imitation learning, where human feedback actively refines a robot’s behavior during training. While interactive imitation learning has shown success in various robotic tasks, its application to dexterous manipulation remains limited. To address this gap, we examine current interactive imitation learning techniques applied to other robotic tasks and discuss how these methods can be adapted to enhance dexterous manipulation. By synthesizing state-of-the-art research, this paper highlights key challenges, identifies gaps in current methodologies, and outlines potential directions for leveraging interactive imitation learning to improve dexterous robotic skills.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this paper, we introduce RoboMIND (Multi-embodiment Intelligence Normative Data for Robot Manipulation), a dataset containing 107k demonstration trajectories across 479 diverse tasks involving 96 object classes. RoboMIND is collected through human teleoperation and encompasses comprehensive robotic-related information, including multi-view observations, proprioceptive robot state information, and linguistic task descriptions. To ensure data consistency and reliability for imitation learning, RoboMIND is built on a unified data collection platform and a standardized protocol, covering four distinct robotic embodiments: the Franka Emika Panda, the UR5e, the AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid robot with dual dexterous hands. Our dataset also includes 5k real-world failure demonstrations, each accompanied by detailed causes, enabling failure reflection and correction during policy learning. Additionally, we created a digital twin environment in the Isaac Sim simulator, replicating the real-world tasks and assets, which facilitates the low-cost collection of additional training data and enables efficient evaluation. To demonstrate the quality and diversity of our dataset, we conducted extensive experiments using various imitation learning methods for single-task settings and state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for multi-task scenarios. By leveraging RoboMIND, the VLA models achieved high manipulation success rates and demonstrated strong generalization capabilities. To the best of our knowledge, RoboMIND is the largest multi-embodiment teleoperation dataset collected on a unified platform, providing large-scale and high-quality robotic training data. Our project is at https://x-humanoid-robomind.github.io/.

## pqac-00000024

From text 'yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3'.

Brian Yang, Jesse Zhang, Vitchyr Pong, Sergey Levine, and Dinesh Jayaraman. Replab: a reproducible low-cost arm benchmark platform for robotic learning. Preprint, Jan 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1905.07447, doi:10.48550/arxiv.1905.07447. This article has 42 citations.

The excerpt describes REPLAB as a low-cost, reproducible benchmarking platform for real-world robotic grasping rather than a mobile-manipulator system. Its portable, self-contained cell combines a six-degree-of-freedom, ceiling-mounted Interbotix WidowX arm, an RGB-D camera, workspace, and protective cage. The platform standardizes the hardware configuration, work-cell design, grasping dataset, baseline software, and performance measures, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons and reproducible evaluation across laboratories. REPLAB cells are designed to be inexpensive, easy to assemble, stackable, scalable to multiple robots, and suitable for crowdsourced or parallelized data collection. The described calibration addresses positioning errors from both the camera and the arm controller. The arm is commanded to target positions on a 5×5 floor grid; actual achieved positions are recorded, and a cell-specific affine model, q = αp + β, is fitted. Target commands are then compensated using p′ = (p − β)/α. For two cells, α values were 0.87 and 0.95, with β set to zero. After compensation, end-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center. The excerpt does not provide the Sulaiman et al. UR5 mobile manipulator’s accuracy.

Calibration and positioning evaluation included stereophotogrammetry for correcting or measuring end-effector pose, which improved pose accuracy by 60% in the cited TIAGO study. NIST’s Configurable Mobile Manipulator Apparatus used coordinate registration, Kalman filtering, and optical tracking to assess pose repeatability and accuracy. A dual-arm system was reported to achieve milligram-level precision for solid dispensing. ## pqac-00000026

From text 'yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3'.

Brian Yang, Dinesh Jayaraman, Jesse Zhang, and Sergey Levine. Replab: a reproducible low-cost arm benchmark for robotic learning. 2019 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), pages 8691-8697, May 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/icra.2019.8794390, doi:10.1109/icra.2019.8794390. This article has 24 citations.

The excerpt describes REPLAB, a low-cost, standardized robotic manipulation platform built around a six-degree-of-freedom WidowX arm from Interbotix Labs, mounted upside down in a portable cell with an RGB-D camera, workspace, and protective cage. Its calibration procedure uses a checkerboard to register robot-coordinate points to 3D camera pixels. Because the cell design and construction protocol are exhaustively specified, the authors state that the same calibration matrix can be reused across cells. They additionally characterize control noise using an affine model, q = αp + β, with α and β learned separately for each cell, and compensate by setting the target to p′ = (p − β)/α. messages.content: Now let me create an artifact with recommended tests for validating a low-cost arm.

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of recommended repeatable tests that could validate a low-cost robot arm (like PiPER or SO-101) for station-to-station calibration in an SDL, based on published protocols. Include columns: Test Name, What is Measured, Protocol (steps), Number of Trials (from literature), Success Criterion, Measuring Tool, Reference System/Arm, Adaptation for Low-Cost Arm. Include these tests:

1. Six-Point Touch Calibration Repeatability (from Burger 2020): Measure how well the arm can recover the position of a known calibration cube after navigating away and returning. 100 trials with ±15mm perturbation. Measuring: cube frame recovery error. Tool: robot contact sensing vs. external measurement. Adapting: use a fixed calibration cube/block and measure how consistently the arm's end-effector returns to it.

2. ArUco/AprilTag Vision Calibration Accuracy (from LIRA/Zhou 2025): Compare vision-based fiducial pose estimation against a reference pose. 100 repetitions. Measuring: translational and rotational error from a known reference position. Tool: wrist camera + ArUco marker + tactile reference. Adapting: mount AprilTags at each station, use wrist camera, compare vision-estimated poses to dial-gauge-verified positions.

3. Microplate Transfer Repeatability (from Harazono 2024): Repeatedly move a microplate (or vial) to a fixed position and measure displacement with dial gauges. 125 trials. Measuring: x/y displacement IQR. Tool: digital dial gauges on aluminum frame. Adapting: use 3D-printed gauge stage with low-cost digital gauges.

4. Workspace Position Accuracy Grid (from REPLAB/Yang 2019): Command the arm to a grid of known targets, measure achieved positions, fit affine correction. 25 targets on 5x5 grid. Measuring: position error across workspace. Tool: checkerboard or AprilTag-measured positions. Adapting: directly applicable to any arm.

5. Lab Vial Pick-and-Place Success Rate (from Johns 2026): Teleoperate demonstrations, train ACT policy, run fixed-start trials. 36 trials. Measuring: binary success/failure of vial placement in holder. Tool: two RGB cameras + visual inspection. Adapting: use LeRobot framework with leader/follower SO-101 arms.

6. Station-to-Station Cycle Test: Drive or move the arm between N stations (simulated by repositioning), recalibrate at each using AprilTag, perform a pick/place task. Measure cumulative success over 50+ cycles. No single published test exactly matches this, but combining Burger's navigate-recalibrate-manipulate cycle with LIRA's visual calibration approach creates a repeatable protocol.

7. Calibration Time Benchmark (from LIRA 2025): Measure time per calibration cycle. LIRA reports ~5s visual vs ~53s tactile. Measuring: seconds per calibration. Tool: timer/software logging."}

{"answer": "# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

The following table summarizes all systems identified in the literature where a robot arm navigates or is repositioned between stations and recalibrates against a local target.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000013). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (pqac-00000000). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (pqac-00000002). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (pqac-00000002). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (pqac-00000001). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (pqac-00000005). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (pqac-00000006). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (pqac-00000020). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (pqac-00000022). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

## 3. AprilTag and ArUco Localization Accuracy at Working Distances

A central question for low-cost arms is how accurately fiducial markers localize at the 0.2–0.5 m distances typical of a wrist camera on a benchtop arm. The following table compiles published accuracy data.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (pqac-00000005).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (pqac-00000034). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (pqac-00000038). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (pqac-00000040). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (pqac-00000040). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (pqac-00000011). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (pqac-00000011). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (pqac-00000015). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (pqac-00000029). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pqac-00000048). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (pqac-00000031). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (pqac-00000032). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (pqac-00000024); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (pqac-00000005).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (pqac-00000006).

## 7. Recommended Tests for Validating a Low-Cost Arm

Based on the published protocols reviewed above, the following table presents a suite of seven repeatable tests that any group can run to compare a low-cost arm against published baselines.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (pqac-00000031).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap."}

{"answer": "# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

The following table summarizes all systems identified in the literature where a robot arm navigates or is repositioned between stations and recalibrates against a local target.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000013). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (pqac-00000000). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (pqac-00000002). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (pqac-00000002). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (pqac-00000001). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (pqac-00000005). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (pqac-00000006). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (pqac-00000020). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (pqac-00000022). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

## 3. AprilTag and ArUco Localization Accuracy at Working Distances

A central question for low-cost arms is how accurately fiducial markers localize at the 0.2–0.5 m distances typical of a wrist camera on a benchtop arm. The following table compiles published accuracy data.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (pqac-00000005).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (pqac-00000034). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (pqac-00000038). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (pqac-00000040). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (pqac-00000040). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (pqac-00000011). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (pqac-00000011). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (pqac-00000015). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (pqac-00000029). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pqac-00000048). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (pqac-00000031). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (pqac-00000032). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (pqac-00000024); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (pqac-00000005).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (pqac-00000006).

## 7. Recommended Tests for Validating a Low-Cost Arm

Based on the published protocols reviewed above, the following table presents a suite of seven repeatable tests that any group can run to compare a low-cost arm against published baselines.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (pqac-00000031).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap."}

At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 62-69). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 2-3). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (brass2026amobilerobotic pages 7-10). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (bavelos2021enablingflexibilityin pages 7-9). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9, sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (bai2026selfbuildinglabs pages 4-7). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

## 3. AprilTag and ArUco Localization Accuracy at Working Distances

The table separates mean error, maximum error, RMSE, and systematic bias because these metrics are not directly interchangeable.*

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (franchini2023mechatronicdesignand pages 6-7). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (wilcock2026fusionoffiducial pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 4-5, lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 5-6). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 1-6). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 6-7, dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 9-10). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8, johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 8-9). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 1-5). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8).

## 7. Recommended Tests for Validating a Low-Cost Arm

Based on the published protocols reviewed above, the following table presents a suite of seven repeatable tests that any group can run to compare a low-cost arm against published baselines.

*Table: A literature-grounded validation suite for comparing affordable PiPER and SO-101 arms with established SDL manipulators. It separates calibration accuracy, loaded repeatability, task success, cycle reliability, timing, and cost so that results are reproducible and failure modes remain visible.*

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

The following table summarizes all systems identified in the literature where a robot arm navigates or is repositioned between stations and recalibrates against a local target.

| Reference | Publication type | Robot arm model | Mobile base / deployment | Calibration target or method | Positioning accuracy after calibration | Trials | Measuring tool / protocol | Calibration time | Station-task tolerance or outcome | DOI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Burger et al. ### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000013). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (pqac-00000000). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (pqac-00000002). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (pqac-00000002). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (pqac-00000001). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (pqac-00000005). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (pqac-00000006). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (pqac-00000020). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (pqac-00000022). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (pqac-00000005).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (pqac-00000034). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (pqac-00000038). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (pqac-00000040). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (pqac-00000040). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (pqac-00000011). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (pqac-00000011). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (pqac-00000015). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (pqac-00000029). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pqac-00000048). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (pqac-00000031). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (pqac-00000032). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (pqac-00000024); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (pqac-00000005).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (pqac-00000006).

*Table: A literature-grounded validation suite for comparing affordable PiPER and SO-101 arms with established SDL manipulators. It separates calibration accuracy, loaded repeatability, task success, cycle reliability, timing, and cost so that results are reproducible and failure modes remain visible.*

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (pqac-00000031).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the KMR mobile robotic chemist’s station/workbench localization as a touch-based six-point calibration method (6P), rather than a camera-based checkerboard calibration. A rigid calibration cube is used as the target, with dimensions of 100 × 100 × 50 mm. The robot physically touches six defined locations on the cube: three points on one plane, two on a perpendicular second plane, and one on a third perpendicular plane. These contacts define the three coordinate planes and their intersection, thereby establishing the cube’s coordinate frame relative to the robot. The method can calibrate object positions relative to the robot or the robot’s position relative to a workbench, supporting re-localization when operating at a station. Testing used 100 separate calibrations while introducing initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation. The cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°. The excerpt specifically reports vial-placement precision and does not mention a checkerboard target or provide a separate station-to-station procedure beyond repeating 6P calibration against the cube/workbench reference.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes LIRA’s ArUco-marker localization preprocessing, but it does not provide the requested quantitative localization accuracy, measurement protocol, number of trials, measuring tool, or achieved localization time. It states that detected markers undergo Gaussian filtering and buffered-detection refinement. Recent marker poses are stored in a buffer; position and orientation are averaged, and the detection closest to the mean pose is selected using Euclidean distance. This is intended to reduce transient errors and produce smoother, more robust pose estimates in dynamic self-driving-laboratory environments. A 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced a mean translational error of 2.42 mm and a mean rotational error of 3.46°. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an evaluation of microplate-transfer positioning repeatability and acceptable placement error using one robot arm: the Dobot M1 Pro fitted with an electric gripper and custom 3D-printed, silicon-rubber-covered fingers. contexts.context: The excerpt reports results for one robot arm: the KUKA LBR iiwa, a seven-degree-of-freedom collaborative arm mounted on the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR). Its specified repeatability is 0.1 mm. The reported positioning evaluation used KUKA’s six-point (6P) touch-sensitive calibration procedure rather than direct microplate measurements. The robot touched a rectangular calibration cube measuring 100 × 100 × 50 mm at six locations: three points defining one plane, two points on a perpendicular plane, and one point on a third perpendicular plane. These contact points were used to calculate the cube’s coordinate frame relative to the robot. The precision test consisted of 100 separate 6P calibrations, with the starting position estimate perturbed by simulated uniform noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation. The measuring tool was therefore the robot’s gripper/contact system touching the calibration cube; no external metrology instrument is identified. The cube was located within 0.12 mm, and orientation offsets were reduced to below 0.005°. The excerpt discusses vial and rack manipulation, not microplate handling, and does not report tests of multiple robot arms. It also notes that cartridge manipulation was not included in the study.

Position repeatability was evaluated by repeatedly grasping a microplate, moving it from its holder to a specified measurement coordinate, pressing the plate against dial-gauge probes to measure x- and y-direction displacement, and returning it to the holder. Success declined gradually with increasing x-offset, while y-direction success decreased sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a reusable platform for evaluating robotic-arm positional repeatability during microplate transfer. The protocol involved transferring a microplate lid while introducing controlled artificial positional offsets in the x and y directions, then determining transfer success by analyzing video images. Offsets ranged from 1.80–2.30 mm in x and 2.10–2.20 mm in y, with 125 transfer trials performed for each offset condition. Success probability decreased progressively as x misalignment increased and declined significantly when y misalignment exceeded 2.190 mm. The platform used an affordable dial gauge to measure positional repeatability; however, the excerpt does not provide the numerical repeatability or accuracy values obtained from that measurement. The physical slope of the microplate and differences in repetitive positioning accuracy were considered influential factors. Only one robot arm was experimentally tested: the Dobot M1 Pro, a SCARA robot. The authors note that results were specific to the hardware and parameters used, and that other robot types—including affordable robots such as the Dobot Magician and myPalletizer, as well as vertical articulated robots—were not tested. Therefore, this excerpt supports the protocol, trial count, measuring tool, and tested robot identity, but not the precise positioning-accuracy figures requested.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe the calibration or re-localization methods used specifically by Dai et al. (2024) or the ARChemist system of Fakhruldeen et al. (2022). It does provide a potentially useful comparison from the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR). The KMR uses a touch-sensitive six-point calibration (6P) procedure to determine the position and orientation of an object or workbench relative to the robot. The target is a rectangular calibration cube measuring 100 × 100 × 50 mm. The robot touches six locations: three points on one plane, two points on a perpendicular second plane, and one point on a third perpendicular plane. These contacts define the coordinate frame through the intersection of the planes and their normal vectors. In testing with simulated initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation, the cube was located within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°. These results concern the KMR and should not be attributed to Dai et al. or ARChemist without consulting those systems’ original publications.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides calibration and positioning details for the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR), relevant to the mobile robotic process chemist. The KMR combines a 7-degree-of-freedom KUKA LBR iiwa robotic arm with an omnidirectional KUKA Mobile Platform. Object and workbench locations are calibrated using a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method (6P). The calibration target is a rectangular cube measuring 100 × 100 × 50 mm. The robot touches the cube at six locations across three mutually perpendicular planes; the recorded contact points are used to calculate a coordinate frame defining the cube’s position and orientation relative to the robot. The method is based on solving plane constraints and perpendicularity relationships, with a pseudoinverse used for an analytical solution. Testing with simulated initial-position noise showed that the cube could be located within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005 degrees. The excerpt does not identify visual fiducial markers such as AprilTags or ArUco markers; instead, it describes a physical calibration cube and direct contact sensing. That system uses eye-in-hand calibration: the robot-mounted camera images a stationary calibration board from multiple robot poses, recording the end-effector pose relative to the robot base and the calibration-board pose in the camera frame. For visual localization, the excerpt specifies ArUco fiducial markers, using the DICT_6X6_50 dictionary, subpixel corner refinement, and single-marker pose estimation. Images are preprocessed with a 5 × 5 Gaussian filter to reduce noise, lighting flicker, motion blur, and marker-edge jitter. The text contrasts this with tactile calibration, which updates the end-effector-to-marker transformation through force-based cube interactions but is slower because it requires sequential movements and sensor validation. contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB as a low-cost, reproducible benchmarking platform for real-world robotic grasping rather than a mobile-manipulator system. Its portable, self-contained cell combines a six-degree-of-freedom, ceiling-mounted Interbotix WidowX arm, an RGB-D camera, workspace, and protective cage. The platform standardizes the hardware configuration, work-cell design, grasping dataset, baseline software, and performance measures, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons and reproducible evaluation across laboratories. REPLAB cells are designed to be inexpensive, easy to assemble, stackable, scalable to multiple robots, and suitable for crowdsourced or parallelized data collection. The described calibration addresses positioning errors from both the camera and the arm controller. The arm is commanded to target positions on a 5×5 floor grid; actual achieved positions are recorded, and a cell-specific affine model, q = αp + β, is fitted. Target commands are then compensated using p′ = (p − β)/α. For two cells, α values were 0.87 and 0.95, with β set to zero. After compensation, end-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center. The excerpt does not provide the Sulaiman et al. UR5 mobile manipulator’s accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB as a low-cost, reproducible benchmarking platform for vision-based robotic manipulation. Its hardware stack includes a robot arm, RGB-D camera, and workspace, costs approximately $2,000, occupies a 70 × 40 × 60 cm cuboid, and can be assembled within a few hours. The platform is intended to make robotics research more accessible and scalable across multiple robots. Rather than focusing on a single arm’s positioning accuracy or calibration procedure, REPLAB establishes a standardized benchmark structure: a task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset containing 92,000 grasp attempts. The paper also reports implementing and evaluating grasping baselines and a deep reinforcement-learning method for 3D reaching on the platform. The broader motivation is to enable apples-to-apples comparisons, reproducibility, rapid replication and improvement, and lower entry barriers, analogous to established reinforcement-learning benchmarks such as ALE and OpenAI Gym.
