contexts.context: The excerpt describes several mobile-manipulator platforms and evaluation methods used in laboratory automation. Burger et al. used a KUKA LBR IIWA arm on a non-holonomic KUKA KMP platform for autonomous navigation and chemical experimentation. The Enabled Robotics Platform combined a MiR200 mobile base with a UR5 arm, while Sulaiman et al. used a Ridgeback omnidirectional platform carrying a 6-DOF Universal Robots UR5e equipped with a Robotiq Hand-E gripper and force-torque sensing. Calibration and positioning evaluation included stereophotogrammetry for correcting or measuring end-effector pose, which improved pose accuracy by 60% in the cited TIAGO study. contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe Sulaiman et al.’s UR5 mobile manipulator, its calibration method, or its positioning accuracy, so no UR5 accuracy value can be established from this material. It does describe REPLAB’s approach to benchmarking low-cost robotic arms. REPLAB is designed as a reproducible, self-contained work cell comprising a commercially available robotic arm, an RGBD camera, and a standardized workspace. The system costs approximately USD 2,000, occupies a 70 × 40 × 60 cm cuboid, and can be assembled within a few hours. Rather than evaluating hardware in isolation, REPLAB defines a complete real-world robotic-learning benchmark for grasping: a standardized task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset containing more than 50,000 grasp attempts. The benchmark is intended to support apples-to-apples comparisons, replication and improvement of research, and wider participation by lowering the cost and engineering burden. The paper also emphasizes scalability to multiple cells and collective robotics, making the platform suitable for collecting data across many standardized low-cost setups. The excerpt contrasts this with prior work that may standardize only objects, datasets, or simulated environments; REPLAB’s contribution is a standardized complete stack for real-world grasping, including the robot, sensors, work-cell design, and evaluation measures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB, a low-cost, standardized robotic manipulation platform built around a six-degree-of-freedom WidowX arm from Interbotix Labs, mounted upside down in a portable cell with an RGB-D camera, workspace, and protective cage. Its calibration procedure uses a checkerboard to register robot-coordinate points to 3D camera pixels. Because the cell design and construction protocol are exhaustively specified, the authors state that the same calibration matrix can be reused across cells. They additionally characterize control noise using an affine model, q = αp + β, with α and β learned separately for each cell, and compensate by setting the target to p′ = (p − β)/α. For the two reported cells, β = 0 and α = 0.87 and 0.95. Combining camera-calibration and residual control errors, end-effector positions are within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace, usually with lower error near the center. REPLAB benchmarks low-cost arms through a standardized grasping task: randomly scattered objects, common RGB-D inputs, and a fixed target grasp configuration, enabling reproducible comparison, scaling across multiple cells, and parallel data collection. contexts.context: The excerpt reports imitation-learning performance for an SO-101 robotic arm, not multiple robot arms. contexts.context: For close-range AprilTag-based pose reconstruction, the paper reports translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm for targets less than 1 m away and rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees (approximately 0.0087 rad). This is the stated performance of the AprilTag/TagSLAM measurement approach, rather than the complete robot arm’s commanded-to-measured positioning accuracy. In the arm experiment, five end-effector points were tested at positions spanning approximately 0.2–0.6 m in the listed coordinates, with the arm reaching each point 10 times. The resulting overall end-effector system accuracy was 0.050 m (5 cm) in position and 0.061 rad (approximately 3.5 degrees) in orientation; lateral positioning accuracy was better than 0.042 m (4.2 cm), and positional repeatability was better than 0.011 m (1.1 cm). The table shows total positional errors of 2.9–5.0 cm and angular systematic errors of 0.002–0.061 rad across P1–P5. Thus, for a wrist-mounted camera or AprilTag localization alone, use the sub-centimeter and sub-0.5-degree figures; for end-effector localization including robot mechanics, calibration, encoder feedback, and execution errors, use the larger 5 cm and 0.061 rad figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports AprilTag performance only at a nearest tested distance of 0.9 m; it does not provide measurements at 0.2 m or explicitly evaluate robot-arm end-effectors or wrist-mounted cameras. In the 0.9 m static trials, AprilTag translational position RMSE (prmse) was 5.11 cm at 0 rad yaw, 5.52 cm at 0.17 rad yaw, and 7.57 cm at −0.34 rad yaw. These correspond to approximately 5.1–7.6 cm three-dimensional position error. The reported coordinate estimates at 0.9 m were approximately x = −4.18 to −3.54 cm, y = 7.46 to 9.02 cm, and z = −2.18 to 8.31 cm, with the listed variability ranging from tenths of a centimeter to several centimeters. Rotational error (qerr) was 0.19, 0.18, and 0.11 rad, respectively—approximately 10.9°, 10.3°, and 6.3°. Thus, based on the available close-range result, AprilTags yielded roughly centimeter-scale-to-several-centimeter translational error and 0.11–0.19 rad rotational error at 0.9 m, but the excerpt cannot establish accuracy across the full 0.2–1.0 m range or for wrist-mounted applications specifically.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a two-stage positioning approach for the mobile manipulator. First, the robot navigates between workstations using laser-sensor data. Because this navigation can introduce positioning error, a camera mounted on the robot performs more accurate localization at the workstation, enabling “virtual docking” without requiring a physical clamping mechanism or special workstation geometry. Cameras mounted on the manipulator then detect the object to be handled, allowing the manipulator to plan and execute the corresponding motion. The software is based on ROS and uses a digital twin (digital world model) that combines the shopfloor layout with real-time sensor and resource information. A task planner uses this model to plan task sequences and communicates with a skill-execution engine/station controller, which executes the required modules. contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe the Bavelos et al. (2021) system specifically, so it provides no verified positioning-accuracy value for that work. In the described mobile manipulator, accurate in-cell task execution is handled through visual docking because ordinary cell-to-cell navigation is sufficient for obstacle avoidance and approximate goal reaching but not for manipulation. Static station re-localization uses a fiducial marker observed by a camera. A proportional visual-servoing controller maintains the robot’s position relative to the marker, with a 20 Hz closed loop. The detected marker pose is transformed from the camera frame to the robot-base frame, making the approach independent of the camera’s mounting location. Position error is converted into traction-system speed commands, while maximum speed and goal tolerances are configurable. The desired docking pose is established during a prior calibration process and stored as the reference goal; the system supports both docking and undocking. Initial Kinect-based detection required a large marker, so a high-resolution IDS camera was installed, improving image quality and accuracy and allowing a smaller marker. For task handling, the robot uses this accurate positioning to support operations such as drilling-pattern detection, sanding alignment, and screwing, while a separate dynamic-docking method is needed when tracking a moving workstation.

contexts.context: The system combines global mobile-robot navigation with precise station-level re-localization before manipulation. The robot moves between workstations using 2D navigation in a pre-mapped shopfloor: laser scanners support SLAM and costmap-based path planning, while dynamic obstacles can trigger path recalculation. Because navigation alone leaves too much error for safe and effective workstation manipulation, the system performs virtual docking after each navigation. Its stereo RealSense camera is used for this docking, but only 2D data is required. The target workstation is identified through a fiducial marker, with AprilTags and Alvar marker families tested. Detection establishes a reference frame for the station; the transformation between the robot frame and marker frame provides the positioning error. A closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm. For sensor installation, camera pose is obtained through hand–eye calibration, relating the camera frame to the mobile robot platform’s base link; the resource manager incorporates this pose and the camera URDF into the robot TF tree. Thus, task handling is structured as navigate to a workstation, visually re-localize/dock accurately, and then enable precise manipulation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes positioning as marker-based visual localization rather than reporting a single numerical accuracy. A fiducial marker at the workstation is used to establish a reference frame; the system calculates the transformation, or position error, between the robot reference frame and the marker. That error is supplied to a closed-loop PID velocity controller, which commands the omnidirectional wheels. Localization finishes when the error falls below an acceptable threshold. PID gains and the finishing criterion are tuned experimentally, providing smooth, fast localization that is described as accurate enough for industrial standards, while allowing accuracy to be reconfigured. The same approach can support conavigation: a camera detects a marker attached to an AGV, allowing the mobile robot to follow it at a specified distance while manipulating objects on the mobile workstation. Task handling uses process perception to compensate for docking deviations and variation in object placement, avoiding reliance on purely preprogrammed manipulator motions. The reported methods include grayscale thresholding, edge detection, and contour comparison, with an AprilTag optionally used as a positional reference relative to the object fixture. Because contours can be unreliable with similar-colored backgrounds or grayscale imagery, the system also tests CAD-model-based 3D surface matching using ICP and PPF methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Dembski et al.’s nanoparticle-production platform as using a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F robotic manipulator, not an ABB YuMi. The arms transfer vessels and materials among a liquid-handling station, dosing station, centrifuge, ultrasonic bath, balance, and other equipment. The stated dosing test ranges were 1–50 g for water and ethanol and 1–20 g for aqueous ammonia. After calibration using an inverse characteristic curve, automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing. In a benchmark, automated dosing was compared with three laboratory technicians, each performing triplicate measurements; automated setpoint deviations were lower, while manual variability depended strongly on the operator. Ammonia was more difficult for both robot and humans because of volatility, motivating a possible closed-vessel solution. For product reproducibility, robot-controlled timing, temperatures, and liquid dosing produced smaller batch-to-batch deviations than manual synthesis. Robot-produced silica nanoparticles had a mean diameter of 206.7 ± 12.0 nm and a PDI of 5.8%, based on manual measurement of 100 SEM particles. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 62-69). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 2-3). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (brass2026amobilerobotic pages 7-10). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (bavelos2021enablingflexibilityin pages 7-9). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9, sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (bai2026selfbuildinglabs pages 4-7). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (franchini2023mechatronicdesignand pages 6-7). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (wilcock2026fusionoffiducial pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 4-5, lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 5-6). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 1-6). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 6-7, dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 9-10). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8, johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 8-9). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 1-5). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8).

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

info.query:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model.
